What is Lux Delux? 
Lux is a nearly 25 year old game that wanted to be Risk online as until that time there were no good versions of the game to play online and pretty much every PC version of the made so far was junk. 
Yes, Risk is a stuffy old board game, how hard could it be to make a PC / Online version of that game?
Well prior to Lux Hasbro a company that over the years has sold nearly 30 million physical copies of the game couldn't figure out how to make the same game fun online. 
Sure, when you played as a kid the game was simplistic (but some might call that easy to learn).  
Sure, playing against your siblings and not so bright cousins as a kid the game may have lost its' challenge by the time you hit puberty. 
So what started out as a essentially as a community project became the best PC version of a game that had been around forever, everyone knew how to play, but somehow nobody could make a decent PC to play. 

Lux solves a lot of those problems by having a plethora of maps and pretty much every variant of Risk that was published by Hasbro and having multiple AI bots that are competent, good, bad and excellent at playing the game. 
On map variety; the purchase of Lux (normally less than $9) gives you access to the 2 expansions; and then you can easily download dozens and dozens of maps and variants in 2 clicks - maps that will work and your don't need to fiddle with or do anything other than DL them for them to show up in your playable game list. 
This point is important as many versions of Risk (including some on Steam versions) will have you pay well over $100 to access all their DLC and maps.  ?WTF? People pay over a $100 to get a bunch of maps for a game that has free versions? 

Anyway Lux in the end is still just good old Risk but its' hassle free and low priced. Yeah the graphics are as simple as the the rules of Risk itself; but that is a bonus as the simple presentation let's you concentrate on just blasting through game after game.  And if you're a fan of any version of risk you likely will play dozens or maybe 100's of games as the AI is what you wish it to be; pick easy opponents for new players and pick killer bot AI for for veterans.

Lux is great bang for your buck if you like risk give a go.

Way back in middle school [i]Risk[/i] was probably my favorite board game, and given that [i]Lux Delux[/i] has apparently been around for two decades it's honestly surprising I've never heard of it until now because I know I would have been obsessed with it. While it's not flashy, this is pretty much the ultimate [i]Risk[/i] experience.

The real magic of [i]Lux Delux[/i] is the absolutely [i]staggering[/i] amount of content for it. That bit on the Steam page that says "over 900" maps actually [i]undersells[/i] it because there's actually over 1000 and so far most of what I've played has been pretty good. There's a plugin menu that lets you sort and manage the different maps, I don't think they're [i]all[/i] installed at the start since it seemed to initially go through a rotation of official ones, but you better believe I opened it up and and installed all of them (coincidentally I think I may have accidentally DDOsD's Sillysoft by doing this, their site seemed to go down shortly after... sorry guys!). The plugin manager is very well organized too, you can sort by name, author, date, and even the ratings people gave to a map.

Trying different maps and seeing the way people push [i]RISK[/i] mechanics to their absolute limit has been a joy. Some of the maps have a highly polished sheen, others are experimental and don't even look like [i]Risk[/i], other are just a crusty JPEG but that doesn't play well at all and the span of two decade's worth of content is honestly just fascinating from a social standpoint so even the lesser maps are interesting. If somebody said "Hey, we made [i]RISK[/i] but you can mod it" nowadays in 2023, I doubt there would have been a ton of content makers flocking to it, aside from perhaps people making their own versions of the game on [i]Tabletop Simulator[/i], but circa 2002, I could [i]totally[/i] see a huge community forming, and making content for it. The latest map in the plugin manager seems dated to 2015 and Sillysoft's forums seem to be down (even before I may have accidentally DDOS'd their site by downloading all the addons. Sorry guys!), so even being a somewhat recent steam release you get the feeling that you're exploring an an abandoned internet community. It's like playing a real-life [i]Risk[/i]-themed version of [i]Hypnospace Outlaw[/i] where every map says a little something about the interests of the people who made it. One map that particularly fascinated me was this big treehouse map which on one hand was cool because it felt like you were playing a room-to-room squad based tactics game, but also because every room and territory was some weird injoke and it was frankly way overdesigned and too granular to really flow well as a [i]Risk[/i] map.

The plugin manager also has info about the maps from the people who made them, and even links to their personal websites, many of which don't even exist anymore, but you can possibly find on the wayback machine. Some infoboxes have shoutouts to other [i]Lux[/i] mappers, who they may have collaborated with or built upon the work of, there's a series of one risk map that got 4 or 5 different versions all tweaked and improved by different people. Sometimes there are little stories, historical information, or just the author writing what inspired them. It's an incredible look into a community that doesn't seem to really be around anymore yet produced a massive amount of work and I really hope the plugin servers stay up so we never lose it. Even just browsing and reading the listings in the manager is deeply interesting, and you can see the game and it's community evolve from the second shareware revolution of the Web 1.0 days, to something to something that became pretty polished and worked it's way into the early days of mobile phone games and survived into modern times, yet seems to have ultimately waned.

But beyond the sociological archaeology of digging through old mods, it's also just a darn good implementation of [i]Risk[/i]. The presentation is minimalistic, you don't even see the dice rolls, but it's fast and to the point and still fun to look at. I had a [i]Risk[/i] game on the PS2 where the characters would constantly talk and make fun of you and it was just tiresome, so I like the directness of it. The AI is also legitimately brilliant. I've had games where I've lost in like two moves and sometimes you just have to sit back and go "wait, where did [i]that[/i] come from?". I feel like I'm actively getting better at [i]Risk[/i] because it's really forcing me to consider all the different strategic aspects of the game. There's one map designed to look like a 200 Meter Olympic swimming pool and the whole thing is just a grid of lanes, and I thought it would be awful but it actually proved to be a brain-wracking math puzzle that I loved and I think the more conceptual maps do a great job really getting you to think about the game and it's mechanics.

I always love when I open a game on a lark and the next thing you know 6 hours have passed. I came into [i]Lux[/i] looking for a good strategy game, and became enamored not only with trying the various content on offer but also digging into the output of its community. This feels like the kind of game that couldn't really be made today, not in the sense that it'd be bad or unappealing, but in the sense that it could have only picked up a community of such size and output by coming out when it did, and by releasing on Steam in 2015 we now have access to that whole two decade's worth of content fully formed,  sorted and organized in one place. Perhaps this is truly the final form of [i]Lux[/i], and maybe it won't grow beyond what it is now, but we have it now and can enjoy it and what it's community left for us, and I hope we never lose that.

[h1] Risking it All [/h1]

Lux Delux is a Risk game where you play on technically an infinite variety of maps and control various "pieces" as you attempt to defeat your opponents. This plays very much like a board game with very little strategy to it. You're going to find yourself just build doom stacks of units and then plowing through enemy territory. At the same time, there is immense satisfaction as you finally plow through enemy stacks and make the entire board your color. The unique boards you can play with that users created can range from plain to superb and complex. Despite having the exact same mechanics every time, seeing these new environments and moving your units throughout them makes you feel like you're conquering completely new areas. Even the hex-based maps that seem to be abundant have their own unique flair to them. This game is not particularly hard, even on hard AI so I recommend at least playing on medium even if you're a more casual gamer.

Still, some of the AIs can feel "cheaty" (I'm not sure if they actually get extra bonuses) as they suddenly have doom stacks of units early into the game and cheaply carve swaths through your territory, sacrificing all their men and security, to prevent only you from getting territory bonuses. There's no diplomacy and the AI will often specifically target you and gang up on you despite that. This game also has a campaign mode. While the objective is always the same, it does present unique scenarios (even you having allies sometimes!) that vary in difficulty. However, each campaign map is still present as unconnected scenarios. There's a decent customization to the scenarios, whether you want more random maps or more "nation vs nation" sorts of things. At the core of it though, it's the same thing over and over again. Overall, if you like Risk, I highly recommend this.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]
[list]
[*]Tons of fun to take over the maps and overwhelm the enemy
[*]Huge variety in map layouts that can provide hours of extra play time
[*]A decent campaign that spices up the game and has unique scenarios
[*]Varied AI that uses their own (predictable) strategies
[*]Easy to get the hang of and large amount of setting customizations
[*]Water is treated as real, equal territories on many maps, as it should be
[/list]
[h1] Cons: [/h1]
[list]
[*]AI can make strange decisions that sometimes feel like they just want to ruin your day
[*]You're going to be technically doing the same thing on every map
[*]Bare-bones graphics, interface, and music
[*]Surprising amount of bugs for such a simple game (beware restarting maps!)
[*]Feels like there's no real strategy involved 
[/list]

[b] Verdict: 7.5/10 [/b]
